summary: Defines SDP offer/answer procedures for negotiating and establishing Binary Floor Control Protocol streams. It obsoletes RFC 4583 and is standards-track.

plainLanguage.summary: Before a meeting can use its "talking stick" system, everyone has to agree on how it will work. This document gives the words to say so in the call setup messages.

questions: how to negotiate bfcp in sdp
what are the bfcp proto values in sdp
subtitle: How call setup messages describe a BFCP stream: the m= line, five new attributes and who plays client or server.

tldr.problem: A BFCP client needs the server's transport address, the conference ID and its user ID before it can connect, and call setup needs a standard way to carry them.
tldr.mechanism: The SDP offer/answer exchange describes a BFCP connection like any other media stream, using an application m= line, five proto values and the floorctrl, confid, userid, floorid and bfcpver attributes.
tldr.outcome: This document obsoletes RFC 4583. It adds UDP and DTLS proto values, a bfcpver attribute and ICE guidance, and drops the c-s role. It is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 8856 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2021. It obsoletes RFC 4583 and pairs with RFC 8855, which it names as the BFCP specification. No later RFC obsoletes or updates it according to the metadata.

sections.title: Why BFCP Needs SDP
sections.content:
As RFC 8855 explains, a BFCP client needs the transport address of the floor control server, the conference identifier and the user identifier before it can connect. One way to get them is an SDP offer/answer exchange. This document specifies how to encode that information in the session descriptions that take part in such an exchange.

The approach is to describe a BFCP connection like any other media stream: with an m= line, possibly followed by other lines that apply to it. The rest of the document defines the m= line fields, five SDP attributes, multiplexing, connection management, TLS and DTLS, ICE, and the offer/answer procedures.
sections.plainLanguage: To join the game, you need to know where it is, which game it is and who you are. This document says how to write that on the invitation.

sections.title: The m= Line and Proto Values
sections.content:
The media field of the m= line must be application. The fmt list is not used by BFCP and must contain a single asterisk character. A port of zero keeps its normal SDP meaning of rejecting the stream. With TCP the port follows the rules in RFC 4145, and an endpoint that will initiate the connection sets it to 9. With UDP the port is where the peer should send BFCP messages.

Five proto values are defined. TCP/BFCP and TCP/TLS/BFCP are backward compatible with endpoints that follow RFC 4583. UDP/BFCP is UDP without DTLS. UDP/TLS/BFCP is UDP with DTLS and is one of the options when ICE is used. TCP/DTLS/BFCP is TCP with DTLS, using the RFC 4571 framing so that a length field precedes each DTLS message; it is the other ICE option.

An example line from the RFC is m=application 50000 TCP/TLS/BFCP followed by the asterisk.
sections.plainLanguage: The first line of the invitation says what kind of thing this is and how to reach it. A few short code words say whether the conversation is locked and which delivery route it uses.

sections.title: The Five SDP Attributes
sections.content:
All five attributes are media-level.

  • floorctrl says which roles the endpoint is willing to take: c-only (floor control client) or s-only (server only). An offer may list both, but an answer must give exactly one, and the offerer takes the opposite role. If the attribute is missing, as with RFC 4583 endpoints, the offerer acts as client and the answerer as server.
  • confid and userid are decimal numbers that a floor control server uses to convey the conference ID and user ID to the client. Their maximum values come from the COMMON-HEADER in RFC 8855.
  • floorid carries a floor ID plus an mstrm: list pointing to the SDP label of each BFCP-controlled media stream.
  • bfcpver lists the BFCP versions supported, matching the Ver field. If absent, it defaults to 1 over a reliable transport and 2 over an unreliable one. The version actually used is conveyed later by the BFCP Hello and HelloAck.

The old c-s value from RFC 4583 was underspecified and implemented inconsistently. Compliant endpoints must not send it but must accept it in an offer, treating it as c-only s-only. Because an answer holds only one role, an endpoint now takes the same role for every BFCP-controlled stream. Receivers are also recommended to parse the misspelling m-stream like mstrm, since some vendors implemented it from an old example.
sections.plainLanguage: The invitation has a few extra labels: who is the helper and who is the guest, which meeting number it is, which seat is yours, which stick controls which screen, and which edition of the rules to use.

sections.title: Offer and Answer Procedures
sections.content:
An initial offer must include floorctrl and bfcpver. If it offers the s-only or c-s role, it must also include confid, userid, floorid and a label on each BFCP-controlled media stream, because the offerer might end up as the server.

An answerer first checks that it supports at least one offered BFCP version; if not, it must not accept the stream. If it accepts, it uses an identical proto value, includes bfcpver with the same or a subset of the offered versions, and includes floorctrl if the offer had one. If it chooses s-only, it supplies the same set of server attributes. To reject, it sets the port to zero and must not set up a TCP or TLS/DTLS connection.

After the answer, the active endpoint initiates the TCP connection and, where relevant, the TLS or DTLS connection by sending a ClientHello. To change the session later, an offerer follows the initial-offer rules, adds connection:existing if it wants to keep an existing TCP connection, and sets the port to zero to disable the stream.
sections.plainLanguage: One side sends an invitation listing what it can do. The other side picks one option, says which rule book edition it will use, and either says yes with its details or says no by writing zero.

sections.title: Connections, TLS, DTLS and ICE
sections.content:
Over UDP, messages go to the address and port in the c= and m= lines. Over TCP, the setup attribute says who initiates the connection and the connection attribute handles re-establishment, and endpoints using offer/answer for TCP must support both. When a connection is closed and re-established, the floor control client must send an offer; if a TCP timeout occurs, the endpoint that detected it must send the offer.

With DTLS over UDP, the generic procedures in RFC 8842 must be followed. With TLS over TCP, the answerer always acts as the TLS server, preserving the RFC 4583 behavior.

For ICE, UDP-based candidates use the UDP/TLS/BFCP procedures and TCP-based candidates use TCP/DTLS/BFCP. All candidate pairs for a stream belong to the same DTLS association, so there is only one DTLS handshake. ICE-enabled endpoints should implement UDP/TLS/BFCP, should include UDP candidates, and should choose the default candidate from those. A BFCP stream must not be part of a BUNDLE group, although BFCP-controlled media streams may be multiplexed.
sections.plainLanguage: Once everyone agrees, one side dials the other. If the line drops, someone sends a new invitation to reconnect. If there are several roads to the meeting, they all count as the same conversation.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
This document points to the security discussions in the BFCP, SDP and offer/answer specifications, and to RFC 4145 and RFC 8122 for TCP and TLS set up via offer/answer. For DTLS over UDP, the generic considerations in RFC 8842 must be followed.

Some proto values produce a BFCP stream that is not protected by TLS or DTLS. In that case operators need to provide integrity and confidentiality protection by other means. The attributes do not reveal the content of the BFCP-controlled streams, but they do reveal which streams will be BFCP controlled.
sections.plainLanguage: Some invitation codes mean the conversation is not locked. If you pick one of those, you have to lock the room another way. Also, the invitation shows which screens have a talking stick, though not what is being said.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 4583
sections.content:
The main goal was signaling support for BFCP over an unreliable transport. The m= line section was rewritten so TCP is no longer the only transport, three proto values were added (TCP/DTLS/BFCP, UDP/BFCP, UDP/TLS/BFCP) and registered with IANA, and the new bfcpver attribute signals the supported version.

The ability to be both client and server at once was removed. Fixes include an erratum about calling attributes media-level, correcting the m-stream spelling to mstrm, and tightening several SHOULDs to MUSTs.
sections.plainLanguage: The new edition adds codes for the quick-mail route, a label for the rule book edition, and removes a confusing option where one person tried to play two roles at once.

m=application 50000 UDP/TLS/BFCP *
a=setup:actpass
a=floorctrl:c-only s-only
a=confid:4321
a=userid:1234
a=floorid:1 mstrm:10
a=floorid:2 mstrm:11
a=bfcpver:1 2
m=audio 50002 RTP/AVP 0
a=label:10
m=video 50004 RTP/AVP 31
a=label:11
